lessons.title: Why Momentum and Mean Reversion Can't Share One Rulebook

body.text: Momentum bets that a move continues. Mean reversion bets that the same move reverses. Run both without regime awareness and one strategy's entry signal is routinely the other's exit signal, on the same stock, on the same day.

children.text: Chapters 2 through 4 built the detection engine: rule-based flags, a fitted HMM, and Markov switching regression. This chapter starts using it. Before building the framework properly, it is worth being precise about exactly why 'just run several strategies together' does not work by default, and momentum versus mean reversion is the cleanest possible illustration of the problem.
Two Opposite Bets on the Same Question

Momentum buys strength and sells weakness, betting that a recent move continues. Mean reversion buys weakness and sells strength, betting that the same move reverses toward some fair value. These are not two flavors of the same idea. They are literal mirror images of each other, applied to the identical input.
Why Both Can Be Right, Just Never at the Same Time

Both sides have genuine, decades-old empirical support. Jegadeesh and Titman's 1993 study documented real, persistent momentum profits in US equities over 3 to 12 month horizons. De Bondt and Thaler's 1985 study documented the opposite pattern over longer horizons, stocks that had performed the worst over several years tending to outperform afterward, evidence of market overreaction correcting itself. Neither paper is wrong. They are describing different regimes and, in part, different horizons: momentum tends to dominate when a genuine trend carries real information forward, the Calm Uptrend or Panic Selloff archetypes from Chapter 1. Mean reversion tends to dominate when price swings reflect noise and liquidity effects oscillating around a stable level, the Range-Bound Chop archetype.
The Cost of Running Both, Unconditionally, at Once

Suppose a desk runs both strategies on the same universe with no regime conditioning at all. On a given day, the momentum model goes long 10,000 shares of a stock trading at Rs 500, and the mean reversion model goes short the same 10,000 shares of the same stock. Netted at the book level, this is zero market exposure. It is not zero cost.

body.label: Cost of two opposing, unconditioned signals that net to zero exposure
body.value: ~Rs 10,000, for no net position at all
body.context: 10,000 shares at Rs 500 is Rs 50 lakh of notional per leg. At an illustrative 10 basis point round-trip cost, brokerage, STT, and slippage combined, each leg costs about Rs 5,000. Two opposing legs cost roughly Rs 10,000 total, for a combined position that carries zero net market exposure.

body.text: A portfolio manager glancing at the netted position sees 'no view' and moves on. What actually happened is two real, individually researched edges cancelled each other out while both paid full transaction costs, a pure drag with no offsetting benefit. This is not a rare edge case; it is the default outcome of running opposed strategies on overlapping universes without any regime conditioning.

children.text: The Fix: Let the Regime Decide Which Rulebook Applies

The resolution is not choosing momentum or mean reversion once and living with the choice, and it is not running both blindly and eating the cancellation cost. It is weighting each strategy by the regime probability built in Chapters 2 through 4: lean into momentum when the fitted model favors a trending regime, lean into mean reversion when it favors a range-bound one, and reduce both when the regime itself looks uncertain or actively transitioning. The next lesson turns this into an explicit framework.

body.text: Momentum and mean reversion are not competing strategies to pick between once. They are correct answers to two different questions, and the regime tells you which question the market is currently asking.

body.title: Diagnosing the Cancellation Problem
body.scenario: A systematic desk runs a momentum strategy and a mean reversion strategy on the same 50-stock universe, with no shared regime signal between them. Reviewing a month of trades, an analyst notices that on 40% of trading days, the two strategies took opposite-direction positions of similar size in the same stock.
body.prompt: What is actually happening on those 40% of days, and what single change would most directly address it?
body.modelAnswer: On those days, the two strategies are reading the same recent price move and reaching opposite conclusions about what it means, one betting on continuation, one betting on reversal, and their positions are partially or fully cancelling each other's market exposure while both still incur full transaction costs on their respective trades. The single most direct fix is to introduce a shared regime signal that both strategies read before sizing their trades, so that momentum's position size scales up and mean reversion's scales down in a trending regime, and vice versa in a range-bound regime, rather than each strategy operating as if the other did not exist.

body.title: Reading the Research Correctly
body.question: Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) documented real momentum profits, and De Bondt and Thaler (1985) documented real long-horizon reversal profits. What is the most accurate way to reconcile these two findings?
options: One of the two studies must be flawed, since they contradict each other
Momentum and reversal are not truly contradictory; they tend to dominate in different regimes and over different horizons, which is exactly why regime conditioning matters
Momentum only works in the United States and reversal only works internationally
The two findings apply to different asset classes entirely, so there is no real tension
body.explanation: Both findings are well-established and neither contradicts the other once regime and horizon are accounted for. Momentum tends to dominate in genuinely trending conditions and reversal tends to dominate when price swings are closer to noise around a stable level, which is precisely the distinction this chapter is built to operationalize rather than resolve by picking a permanent winner.

points: Momentum and mean reversion are literal mirror images: the same observed price move produces opposite trading decisions under each

Both have genuine, decades-old empirical support, Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) for momentum, De Bondt and Thaler (1985) for reversal, describing different regimes and horizons rather than contradicting each other
Running both strategies unconditionally on an overlapping universe routinely produces opposing trades that cancel exposure while both legs still pay full transaction costs
An illustrative Rs 50 lakh notional position cancelled this way can cost roughly Rs 10,000 in transaction costs for zero net market exposure gained
The fix is regime-conditional weighting, not a permanent choice between the two strategies, which the rest of this chapter builds out explicitly
